note.text: A main idea states what the passage principally says about its topic. A topic names the subject but does not express the claim. Supporting details explain, illustrate or justify the main idea. A good main-idea statement covers the relevant details without adding a conclusion the passage does not support. It need not reproduce an opening sentence word for word.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to select a passage’s controlling idea and distinguish it from evidence or an unsupported claim. Builds on: Form Five evidence-based reading. Leads to: purpose, summary and inference.

sections.heading: Read the original model
sections.text: Original passage: The fictional school library changed its loan routine after pupils reported long queues. Volunteers sorted returns before the break, and borrowers placed requests on slips. The trial shortened some queues, but staff had not yet compared all weekdays. The passage describes a trial with a limited reported result, rather than proving every queue problem is solved.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: State the topic, ask what the writer says about it, then test a proposed main idea against the whole passage. Identify which detail supports it and which limitation it must retain.

cards.idea: Read the whole example before identifying its function.

cards.idea: A correction must preserve the intended meaning and form.
example: A topic label alone expresses every argument. Correction: A main idea says something about the topic.
The passage proves every library needs identical slips. Correction: The trial’s context and limited evidence must be preserved.
A single detail is always the entire main idea. Correction: A detail supports a broader point rather than necessarily replacing it.
An early result guarantees permanent success. Correction: The passage explicitly limits the comparison.

pick.q: Original passage: Bih’s club tested shaded seating. Members used it at midday, but rainy-day use was not recorded. Which main idea preserves scope?
pick.r: A seating trial attracted midday use, with evidence still limited
w: Every school must build the same seats
e: Rainy-day evidence is missing.
The trial does not establish a universal requirement.
Ownership is not stated.
pick.y: Cover both the observed use and the evidence limit.

pick.q: Original passage: A fictional market team labelled separate collection bins and explained the labels. Sorting improved during observed mornings; afternoon use remains unknown. Which is the main idea?
pick.r: A labelling-and-explanation trial improved observed sorting, with incomplete coverage
w: The only topic is the colour of paper
e: The passage concerns a sorting intervention.
Only a limited observation is reported.
Afternoon use was not observed.
pick.y: A main idea covers intervention, result and limitation.

pick.q: Original passage: Ayuk’s group shared a timetable to avoid room clashes. Reported clashes fell, though the group had no record of informal meetings. Which statement fits the whole passage?
pick.r: A shared timetable reduced reported clashes but the record was incomplete
e: Missing records do not prove absence.
The reported change concerns the timetable.
The claim exceeds the reported evidence.
pick.y: Keep the central change without turning incomplete records into certainty.
